status_summary: Executive Order 14321 (2025-07-24) directed HUD and HHS to end support for Housing First policies and to raise treatment conditions. HUD's FY2025 Continuum of Care notice (November 2025) was challenged by states and cities; the Rhode Island court's order of 2026-06-29 vacated HUD's November and December 2025 notices (per the court's later opinion), and HUD awarded FY2025 renewals in 2026 (about $3.85 billion across three rounds, per HUD). HUD's FY2026 notice of 2026-06-01 offers about $4.04 billion, sets aside about $1.3 billion (roughly 30 percent) for new transitional-housing and services-only projects, makes 60 percent of annual renewal demand available in tier 1 (the minimum the FY2026 appropriations law requires), and adds scoring points for treatment and recovery services (up to 20 of 200) and for requiring participation in supportive services (up to 8), according to the Congressional Research Service. On 2026-08-07 the district court (Judge McElroy, D.R.I.) set aside the FY2026 notice in its entirety because HUD issued the set-aside without the notice and comment the statute requires, declined to enjoin future versions, and did not reach the other challenges or rule on the merits of the policy shift; HUD may reissue similar conditions after notice and comment. HUD appealed on 2026-08-13, the First Circuit stayed the vacatur on 2026-09-16 (Nos. 26-1922 and 26-1923), and HUD reopened the notice on 2026-09-18 with applications due 2026-09-30. JURIST reports the stay order found HUD likely to succeed on the view that the set-aside is not an incentive subject to the comment requirement and that HUD must award funds by 2026-12-01. Plaintiffs then asked the First Circuit to vacate the ruling and remand or expedite the appeal, and no decision on that motion was reported as of 2026-09-22. HUD has used funding notices rather than a rule change or new statute, and permanent housing renewals remain funded.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14321 signed; Section 5 directs HUD and HHS to end support for Housing First policies and HUD to increase treatment requirements for participants with substance use disorder or serious mental illness.

A state coalition sues over HUD's FY2025 Continuum of Care notice (issued in November 2025, which de-emphasized Housing First); a separate suit by cities and nonprofits follows on 2025-12-01. A court enters a preliminary injunction in December 2025 and HUD withdraws and later reopens the prior-year notice.

HUD announces the first round of FY2025 Continuum of Care renewal awards ($349 million for 622 projects); later rounds follow on 2026-04-27 and 2026-05-21, totaling about $3.85 billion, under the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (Public Law 119-75).
HUD abandons its appeal of the December 2025 preliminary injunction (month only known; reported by the California Attorney General, so dated to the first of the month).

HUD issues the FY2026 Continuum of Care NOFO: about $4.04 billion total, about $1.3 billion (roughly 30 percent) set aside for new transitional-housing and services-only projects, 60 percent of annual renewal demand available in tier 1 (the statutory minimum), and scoring points for treatment and recovery services and for requiring participation in supportive services (CRS). A lawsuit follows on 2026-07-02 and HUD modifies the notice on 2026-07-24.

D.R.I. Judge Mary McElroy rules HUD's 2025 overhaul of the program violated the Administrative Procedure Act and vacates HUD's November and December 2025 NOFOs (per the court's 2026-08-07 background); she declines to bar similar future changes or to fold the FY2026 notice into the same case (Maryland Matters).

Judge McElroy (State of Washington v. HUD, 1:26-cv-00439; NAEH v. HUD, 1:26-cv-00436) grants summary judgment in part and sets aside the FY2026 NOFO in its entirety: the roughly $1.3 billion set-aside requires notice and comment under 42 U.S.C. 11386b(d)(2)(C), which HUD did not provide; the court denies a permanent injunction against future versions, does not reach the other challenges (including OMB apportionment footnotes) and does not rule on whether the policy shift from Housing First is lawful on its merits. HUD appeals on 2026-08-13.
timeline.source: U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island (via govinfo)

timeline.event: A First Circuit panel (Nos. 26-1922 and 26-1923, consolidated) grants HUD a stay pending appeal of the district court's vacatur, per HUD and CRS; HUD reopens the FY2026 NOFO on 2026-09-18 with a 2026-09-30 deadline.

Plaintiffs (National Alliance to End Homelessness) file an emergency motion in the First Circuit asking it to vacate the district court ruling and remand so other claims can be heard, or alternatively to expedite the appeal; no ruling reported. The First Circuit stay order found HUD likely to succeed on the argument that the $1.3 billion set-aside is not a bonus or incentive covered by the comment requirement, and HUD has until 2026-12-01 to award the funds.
timeline.source: National Alliance to End Homelessness / JURIST

uncertainties: Sources conflict on what HUD did in December 2025: the California Attorney General and a law-firm summary say a preliminary injunction required HUD to keep the prior-year NOFO and HUD reopened it in January 2026, while Smart Cities Dive describes a December reissue with similar policy changes and Maryland Matters reports a new NOFO on 2025-12-19; the Rhode Island court's 2026-08-07 opinion says its 2026-06-29 order vacated both the November and December 2025 notices, but the 2025 and June 2026 orders themselves were not read. The August 2026 opinion and the CRS Insight were read through fetch summaries; the First Circuit stay order was not read (the Leagle page shows only an introduction), so its reasoning and the 2026-12-01 award deadline rest on JURIST. The exact date of the November 2025 NOFO is as reported by news outlets. HUD's page says the district court ruled to 'vacate' the FY2026 notice and the court's order says it set the notice aside. The CRS Insight gives the FY2026 notice release as 2026-06-01, a lawsuit on 2026-07-02, a HUD modification on 2026-07-24 and HUD's appeal on 2026-08-13; the plaintiffs' emergency motion date may be 2026-09-21 rather than 2026-09-22. Nothing after 2026-10-02 on the First Circuit appeal was found. A separate HUD Federal Register notice on incentivized homelessness-reduction activities (comments due 2026-10-13) was not read. No rule change to 24 CFR part 578 and no statute was located.
